Overwhelmed? Stressed? No, no, I wouldn't say that at all. It's more like... I just wish people would either get on board with what I'm doing or get out of my way! Well, I guess that depends on what you mean by consequences. I already told you about the deposits, right? Well, I don't really know if it's changed, to be honest. Have I always been like this? I guess it depends on how you look at it. I mean, what does 'always' even mean at my age? Time is a funny thing when you get to be seventy-four. 

It's like when I was taking a few college classes back in the early seventies. I took this history course—European History, I think it was. The professor, Dr. Harrison, he used to smoke a pipe right there in the lecture hall! Can you imagine someone doing that today? The fire alarms would be going off, they'd evacuate the building! But back then, the smoke would just catch the light from the overhead projector, swirling around while he talked about the Industrial Revolution. Which is funny, really, because I ended up working in a plant my whole life anyway. Mixing and grinding, breathing in dust instead of cherry tobacco smoke. 

But back in those days, you know, things were just different. We'd just decide to drive down to the shore on a Tuesday afternoon. My buddy Jimmy had a Ford Pinto. Terrible car, a real fire hazard if you got rear-ended, but it was mustard yellow and we loved it. We'd roll the windows down and listen to the 8-track player. He had this one tape that always got stuck on the third song. You had to smack the dashboard right above the radio with the heel of your hand to get it to switch tracks. Jimmy actually broke his watch doing that once. 

So, I don't know about changing over time or acting on impulse. I've always just kind of done what makes sense at the exact moment, you know? You just gotta keep moving.

I'm just trying to get things done!\n\nDoctor: Do you find that your mood changes quickly, from feeling very good to very bad, without much of a reason?\n\nPatient: Well, yeah, I guess I did mention that before, didn't I? It's exactly like that. One minute I'm on top of the world, feeling ten feet tall, making jokes with the guys—like that termite joke, you know, a termite walks into a bar and asks, 'Is the bar tender?' Always gets a chuckle! But then, boom, my wife or my son asks me some tiny little question about the move, and I just snap at them. I mean, I really let 'em have it. I just feel like everybody needs to either get on board with my plans or get out of my way! \n\nIt's like when we were pouring the concrete for the patio at the old house back in '05. We had the cement truck out there, and the driver—big guy, wore suspenders with little tools printed on them—he was taking his sweet time backing up. I'm standing there with the float, ready to smooth it out, and the sun is beating down, and concrete doesn't wait for anybody! You gotta work it while it's wet! I started yelling at him to hurry up, and my wife came out with lemonade, and I ended up yelling at her too. She dropped the tray, broke two of our good glasses. The ones with the little etched flowers on them. We got those for our anniversary... our fifteenth, I think? No, twentieth. Anyway, it's just like that. I'm fine, joking around, and then suddenly I'm biting someone's head off because they aren't moving fast enough!\n\nDoctor: Have you always been someone who acts on impulse, or is this something that has changed for you over time?\n\nPatient: Well, I don't really know if it's changed, to be honest. Have I always been like this? I guess it depends on how you look at it. I mean, what does 'always' even mean at my age? Time is a funny thing when you get to be seventy-four. \n\nIt's like when I was taking a few college classes back in the early seventies. I took this history course—European History, I think it was. The professor, Dr. Harrison, he used to smoke a pipe right there in the lecture hall! Can you imagine someone doing that today? The fire alarms would be going off, they'd evacuate the building! But back then, the smoke would just catch the light from the overhead projector, swirling around while he talked about the Industrial Revolution. Which is funny, really, because I ended up working in a plant my whole life anyway. Mixing and grinding, breathing in dust instead of cherry tobacco smoke. \n\nBut back in those days, you know, things were just different. We'd just decide to drive down to the shore on a Tuesday afternoon. My buddy Jimmy had a Ford Pinto. Terrible car, a real fire hazard if you got rear-ended, but it was mustard yellow and we loved it. We'd roll the windows down and listen to the 8-track player. He had this one tape that always got stuck on the third song. You had to smack the dashboard right above the radio with the heel of your hand to get it to switch tracks. Jimmy actually broke his watch doing that once. \n\nSo, I don't know about changing over time or acting on impulse. I've always just kind of done what makes sense at the exact moment, you know? You just gotta keep moving.\n\n[Last Question]\nWould you say that acting on impulse without thinking things through is something that you've done your whole life?\n\n[Patient Info]\n- demographics: Male / 74 / crushing_grinding_polishing_mixing_or_blending_worker / some_college\n- severity: Severe\n\n[Targeted Info]\nNone\n\n[Conversation Style]\nYou are a Tangent patient.\nA patient who goes off on tangents may\n1) begin answering the doctor's question but quickly shift to an unrelated topic,\n2) frequently add irrelevant personal anecdotes or experiences while answering the question, and\n3) have difficulty remaining focused on the doctor's question, potentially requiring the doctor to repeat the question or redirect the conversation to obtain clear clinical information.\nThis is how you are, not a performance you put on in every reply — let it show as much or as little as the moment calls for.\n\nWhat to do:\n- Answer the doctor's last question with what [Targeted Info] holds, in your own words.\n- You are speaking out loud, not reading a line you prepared. ========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Well, my whole life? I don't know if I'd say my *whole* life. I mean, what does it mean to think things through anyway? You can plan and plan and plan, and then it rains. 

Like when we were supposed to go to my sister's wedding back in '82. We had the route all mapped out—this was before GPS, you know, when you had to use those big fold-out paper maps from the gas station. The ones you could never fold back up the right way. My wife used to get so mad when I'd just shove it in the glove compartment all crumpled up. The glove compartment on that old Buick LeSabre was huge, though. You could fit three flashlights, a tire gauge, and a whole box of tissues in there. We used to keep those little peppermints wrapped in the clear plastic in there too. They'd get all soft in the summer heat. 

Anyway, we had it all planned, and then the alternator went out right outside of Columbus. Just died on the highway. So much for thinking things through, right? Sometimes you just have to act on what's right in front of you. You just gotta fix the alternator or buy a new car. Actually, we ended up getting towed to this little shop where the mechanic had a three-legged dog. Sweetest thing, a golden retriever mix. It would hop right up to you and rest its chin on your knee while you waited. 

So, yeah, I don't know about the whole impulse thing. I just do what needs doing when it needs doing.

Well, younger... I mean, when you're young you do things, sure. But lately? Lately it's just been about getting things done. Like with the move. Best dog we ever had, used to chase the mailman right down to the corner... \n\nBut anyway, she says I'm not thinking. And the guys at the plant, too. I've been rushing some of the mixing jobs, just to get them done, and driving back and forth between the old house and the new one like a madman. They keep telling me I'm taking chances, going too fast, but if I slow down, I lose the momentum! You know what happens to a grinding wheel when it loses momentum? It bogs down. Just ruins the whole batch. You have to keep the RPMs up. That's just basic physics, which I learned back at the community college. Professor Higgins, he was a tough old bird, but he knew his stuff...\n\nDoctor: Are you feeling overwhelmed or stressed by all the things you're trying to get done?\n\nPatient: Overwhelmed? Stressed? No, no, I wouldn't say that at all. It's more like... I just wish people would either get on board with what I'm doing or get out of my way! I mean, one minute I'm feeling fantastic, ten feet tall, making jokes with the guys at the lumber yard—there was this one joke about a termite and a bartender, always gets a laugh—and then the next minute, my wife or my boy asks me some little, insignificant question about the moving boxes, and I just snap at them. I don't mean to, but they just don't see the big picture! \n\nLike the other day, my son comes over. Good kid, he's an accountant now, wears a suit every day. Can you imagine? I spent my whole life in work boots and coveralls, covered in dust from the grinding room, and he's sitting in an air-conditioned office looking at spreadsheets. Not that I'm not proud of him, I am. He bought this nice house out in the suburbs, got a golden retriever. But he comes over and starts asking me if I've labeled the boxes for the kitchen. Labeled the boxes! I've got a whole system in my head, I don't need a label maker to tell me where the toaster goes! So I yelled at him. Told him to go back to his spreadsheets and leave the real work to me. He looked at me like I was crazy. But I'm just trying to get it all done, you know? If they'd just let me work...\n\nDoctor: Do you often act on impulse without considering the consequences?\n\nPatient: Well, I guess that depends on what you mean by consequences. I already told you about the deposits, right? Yeah, I put down all that money for the new garage foundation and the equipment without running it by my wife first. She was furious. But like I said, you gotta strike while the iron is hot! I used to tell that to the new guys at the plant. We'd get these young kids, fresh out of high school, looking at the grinding machines like they were spaceships. I always told them, 'You gotta commit to the cut!' If you hesitate, you ruin the material. \n\nAnd speaking of the plant, I've been rushing through some of those mixing jobs lately. Just trying to get it done so I can get back to the house stuff. The supervisor—Dave, nice guy, but a real stickler for the rules, always wears his hard hat perfectly straight—he told me I was taking chances. Said I was going too fast. And then I'm in the truck, driving back and forth between the old house and the new one, trying to beat the traffic on I-95. The guys at work said I was driving like a maniac, but they just don't understand how much I have to do! I've been making that drive for thirty years, I know every pothole on that highway. There's this one right near the exit for the diner—the one that makes the best blueberry pancakes, you know the place? My wife and I used to go there every Sunday after church. Anyway, I know what I'm doing. I'm just trying to keep the momentum going.\n\nDoctor: Are you having trouble getting along with your family or coworkers because of your behavior?\n\nPatient: Well, it's... it's gotten a bit complicated, I suppose. At work, they actually pulled me off the floor. Had a little safety incident because I was moving so fast, and Dave—the supervisor I mentioned, the one with the straight hard hat—he said I couldn't be on the machines right now. It's a shame, really, because those machines need a certain touch. You can't just put anybody on a grinder. I remember when we got the new models back in '98, took me three weeks just to figure out the vibration patterns. You have to listen to the hum of the motor, you know? It sings to you if it's running right. \n\nBut anyway, yeah, work's a problem right now. And at home... well, my wife and the kids, they've basically cut me out of the loop. They don't trust me with the money anymore, after the garage deposits. And they don't want me driving, either. My wife hid my keys the other day! Can you believe that? Hid the keys to my own truck! It's a Chevy Silverado, 2015, runs like a dream. I change the oil myself every three thousand miles, wouldn't trust those quick-lube places if you paid me. They always try to upcharge you for wiper blades. But now she's saying things have just gotten out of hand with the move and everything, so they're trying to manage it all without me. It's frustrating, you know? I'm just trying to get things done!\n\nDoctor: Do you find that your mood changes quickly, from feeling very good to very bad, without much of a reason?\n\nPatient: Well, yeah, I guess I did mention that before, didn't I? It's exactly like that. One minute I'm on top of the world, feeling ten feet tall, making jokes with the guys—like that termite joke, you know, a termite walks into a bar and asks, 'Is the bar tender?' Always gets a chuckle! But then, boom, my wife or my son asks me some tiny little question about the move, and I just snap at them. I mean, I really let 'em have it. I just feel like everybody needs to either get on board with my plans or get out of my way! \n\nIt's like when we were pouring the concrete for the patio at the old house back in '05. We had the cement truck out there, and the driver—big guy, wore suspenders with little tools printed on them—he was taking his sweet time backing up. I'm standing there with the float, ready to smooth it out, and the sun is beating down, and concrete doesn't wait for anybody! You gotta work it while it's wet! I started yelling at him to hurry up, and my wife came out with lemonade, and I ended up yelling at her too. She dropped the tray, broke two of our good glasses. The ones with the little etched flowers on them. We got those for our anniversary... our fifteenth, I think? No, twentieth. Anyway, it's just like that. I'm fine, joking around, and then suddenly I'm biting someone's head off because they aren't moving fast enough!\n\nDoctor: Have you always been someone who acts on impulse, or is this something that has changed for you over time?\n\nPatient: Well, I don't really know if it's changed, to be honest. Have I always been like this? I guess it depends on how you look at it. I mean, what does 'always' even mean at my age? Time is a funny thing when you get to be seventy-four. \n\nIt's like when I was taking a few college classes back in the early seventies. I took this history course—European History, I think it was. The professor, Dr. Harrison, he used to smoke a pipe right there in the lecture hall! Can you imagine someone doing that today? The fire alarms would be going off, they'd evacuate the building! But back then, the smoke would just catch the light from the overhead projector, swirling around while he talked about the Industrial Revolution. Which is funny, really, because I ended up working in a plant my whole life anyway. Mixing and grinding, breathing in dust instead of cherry tobacco smoke. \n\nBut back in those days, you know, things were just different. We'd just decide to drive down to the shore on a Tuesday afternoon. My buddy Jimmy had a Ford Pinto. Terrible car, a real fire hazard if you got rear-ended, but it was mustard yellow and we loved it. We'd roll the windows down and listen to the 8-track player. He had this one tape that always got stuck on the third song. You had to smack the dashboard right above the radio with the heel of your hand to get it to switch tracks. Jimmy actually broke his watch doing that once. \n\nSo, I don't know about changing over time or acting on impulse. I've always just kind of done what makes sense at the exact moment, you know? You just gotta keep moving.\n\nDoctor: Would you say that acting on impulse without thinking things through is something that you've done your whole life?\n\nPatient: Well, my whole life? I don't know if I'd say my *whole* life. I mean, what does it mean to think things through anyway? You can plan and plan and plan, and then it rains. \n\nLike when we were supposed to go to my sister's wedding back in '82. We had the route all mapped out—this was before GPS, you know, when you had to use those big fold-out paper maps from the gas station. The ones you could never fold back up the right way. My wife used to get so mad when I'd just shove it in the glove compartment all crumpled up. The glove compartment on that old Buick LeSabre was huge, though. You could fit three flashlights, a tire gauge, and a whole box of tissues in there. We used to keep those little peppermints wrapped in the clear plastic in there too. They'd get all soft in the summer heat. \n\nAnyway, we had it all planned, and then the alternator went out right outside of Columbus. Just died on the highway. So much for thinking things through, right? Sometimes you just have to act on what's right in front of you. You just gotta fix the alternator or buy a new car. Actually, we ended up getting towed to this little shop where the mechanic had a three-legged dog. Sweetest thing, a golden retriever mix. It would hop right up to you and rest its chin on your knee while you waited. \n\nSo, yeah, I don't know about the whole impulse thing. I just do what needs doing when it needs doing.\n\nDoctor: Would you describe yourself as someone who has always acted on impulse, even when you were younger?\n\nPatient: Well, younger... I mean, when you're young you do things, sure. But lately? Lately it's just been about getting things done. Like with the move. I just went ahead and put deposits down on all this garage work and bought equipment for the new place. Didn't even talk it over with my wife, which, well, she wasn't too happy about that. But you have to strike while the iron is hot! Just like at the plant. I've been rushing jobs there, trying to get everything finished up so I can focus on the move. People keep telling me I'm taking chances, moving too fast with the machinery, but they don't understand the schedule I'm on. \n\nI've been driving back and forth between the old house and the new one, too. Just back and forth, back and forth. The new house has this big oak tree in the front yard. Massive thing. Reminds me of the tree we had when I was a kid growing up on Elm Street. Ironically, it wasn't an elm tree, it was a maple. We used to tap it for syrup in the winter. My dad had these little metal buckets he'd hang on the spiles. You'd hear the drip, drip, drip all day if it was quiet enough. We'd boil it down on the stove and the whole house would smell sweet and sticky for a week. My mother hated it because it made the wallpaper peel in the kitchen. She had this yellow wallpaper with little roosters on it. So tacky, looking back on it, but that was the style then. Everything was roosters or apples. \n\nAnyway, what was I saying? Oh, right, the deposits. Yeah, I just paid 'em. You can't wait around for people to make up their minds, you know?\n\nDoctor: Would you say that acting on impulse has always been a part of your personality, even before this recent period of stress with the move?\n\nPatient: Well, no, not always. Plus, the bugs down there are the size of your fist! My brother-in-law lived in Tampa for a few years and he said he found a palmetto bug in his shoe once. Can you imagine? You go to put your shoe on and crunch! \n\nBut yeah, it's just been this last month with the house situation. Well, like I was trying to say, it's really just been this last month. You know, since we got the news that we were being forced to start leaving the old house. It's not like I've been doing this my whole life! But when you have a deadline hanging over your head... 

Speaking of deadlines, the post office has been an absolute nightmare with the change of address forms. You'd think in this day and age, with all the computers, they could just press a button and know where I live. But no, I had to fill out this little card, and the pen they had chained to the desk—why do they chain them? Who is stealing those cheap little plastic pens? Anyway, it was completely out of ink. Just scratched a groove right into the paper. I had to go back out to the truck to find one, and then I ended up finding that old flashlight I thought I lost back in November. The one with the heavy metal casing that takes the big D batteries. You don't see flashlights like that much anymore. Now everything is those tiny LED things. They're bright, sure, but they don't feel substantial in your hand, you know? If you had to break a window in an emergency, one of those little plastic things wouldn't do you any good. 

But yeah, it's just been the last month or so, since the whole house thing started. Before that, everything was perfectly normal.

I feel like we're going in circles here, Doc! Like I said, it's just been the last month. About a month, yeah. Ever since we found out we were being forced to start leaving the old house. It's not a lifelong habit, I promise you. 

Though, speaking of habits, I used to have this terrible habit of chewing on the end of my pencils when I was in college. Just gnawing them down to the metal part where the eraser used to be. I took a few classes over at the community college—business administration, thought I might want to run my own shop someday. Never panned out, ended up at the plant instead, grinding and polishing. The supervisor—Dave, nice guy, but a real stickler for the rules, always wears his hard hat perfectly straight—he told me I was taking chances. Said I was going too fast. And then I'm in the truck, driving back and forth between the old house and the new one, trying to beat the traffic on I-95. The guys at work said I was driving like a maniac, but they just don't understand how much I have to do! I've been making that drive for thirty years, I know every pothole on that highway. There's this one right near the exit for the diner—the one that makes the best blueberry pancakes, you know the place? My wife and I used to go there every Sunday after church. Anyway, I know what I'm doing. I'm just trying to keep the momentum going.\n\nDoctor: Are you having trouble getting along with your family or coworkers because of your behavior?\n\nPatient: Well, it's... it's gotten a bit complicated, I suppose. At work, they actually pulled me off the floor. Had a little safety incident because I was moving so fast, and Dave—the supervisor I mentioned, the one with the straight hard hat—he said I couldn't be on the machines right now. It's a shame, really, because those machines need a certain touch. You can't just put anybody on a grinder. I remember when we got the new models back in '98, took me three weeks just to figure out the vibration patterns. You have to listen to the hum of the motor, you know? It sings to you if it's running right. \n\nBut anyway, yeah, work's a problem right now. And at home... well, my wife and the kids, they've basically cut me out of the loop. They don't trust me with the money anymore, after the garage deposits. And they don't want me driving, either. My wife hid my keys the other day! Can you believe that? Hid the keys to my own truck! It's a Chevy Silverado, 2015, runs like a dream. I change the oil myself every three thousand miles, wouldn't trust those quick-lube places if you paid me. They always try to upcharge you for wiper blades. But now she's saying things have just gotten out of hand with the move and everything, so they're trying to manage it all without me. It's frustrating, you know? I'm just trying to get things done!\n\nDoctor: Do you find that your mood changes quickly, from feeling very good to very bad, without much of a reason?\n\nPatient: Well, yeah, I guess I did mention that before, didn't I? It's exactly like that. One minute I'm on top of the world, feeling ten feet tall, making jokes with the guys—like that termite joke, you know, a termite walks into a bar and asks, 'Is the bar tender?' Always gets a chuckle! But then, boom, my wife or my son asks me some tiny little question about the move, and I just snap at them. I mean, I really let 'em have it. I just feel like everybody needs to either get on board with my plans or get out of my way! \n\nIt's like when we were pouring the concrete for the patio at the old house back in '05. We had the cement truck out there, and the driver—big guy, wore suspenders with little tools printed on them—he was taking his sweet time backing up. I'm standing there with the float, ready to smooth it out, and the sun is beating down, and concrete doesn't wait for anybody! You gotta work it while it's wet! I started yelling at him to hurry up, and my wife came out with lemonade, and I ended up yelling at her too. She dropped the tray, broke two of our good glasses. The ones with the little etched flowers on them. We got those for our anniversary... our fifteenth, I think? No, twentieth. Anyway, it's just like that. I'm fine, joking around, and then suddenly I'm biting someone's head off because they aren't moving fast enough!\n\nDoctor: Have you always been someone who acts on impulse, or is this something that has changed for you over time?\n\nPatient: Well, I don't really know if it's changed, to be honest. Have I always been like this? I guess it depends on how you look at it. I mean, what does 'always' even mean at my age? Time is a funny thing when you get to be seventy-four. \n\nIt's like when I was taking a few college classes back in the early seventies. I took this history course—European History, I think it was. The professor, Dr. Harrison, he used to smoke a pipe right there in the lecture hall! Can you imagine someone doing that today? The fire alarms would be going off, they'd evacuate the building! But back then, the smoke would just catch the light from the overhead projector, swirling around while he talked about the Industrial Revolution. Which is funny, really, because I ended up working in a plant my whole life anyway. Mixing and grinding, breathing in dust instead of cherry tobacco smoke. \n\nBut back in those days, you know, things were just different. We'd just decide to drive down to the shore on a Tuesday afternoon. My buddy Jimmy had a Ford Pinto. Terrible car, a real fire hazard if you got rear-ended, but it was mustard yellow and we loved it. We'd roll the windows down and listen to the 8-track player. He had this one tape that always got stuck on the third song. You had to smack the dashboard right above the radio with the heel of your hand to get it to switch tracks. Jimmy actually broke his watch doing that once. \n\nSo, I don't know about changing over time or acting on impulse. I've always just kind of done what makes sense at the exact moment, you know? You just gotta keep moving.\n\nDoctor: Would you say that acting on impulse without thinking things through is something that you've done your whole life?\n\nPatient: Well, my whole life? I don't know if I'd say my *whole* life. I mean, what does it mean to think things through anyway? You can plan and plan and plan, and then it rains. \n\nLike when we were supposed to go to my sister's wedding back in '82. We had the route all mapped out—this was before GPS, you know, when you had to use those big fold-out paper maps from the gas station. The ones you could never fold back up the right way. My wife used to get so mad when I'd just shove it in the glove compartment all crumpled up. The glove compartment on that old Buick LeSabre was huge, though. You could fit three flashlights, a tire gauge, and a whole box of tissues in there. We used to keep those little peppermints wrapped in the clear plastic in there too. They'd get all soft in the summer heat. \n\nAnyway, we had it all planned, and then the alternator went out right outside of Columbus. Just died on the highway. Actually, we ended up getting towed to this little shop where the mechanic had a three-legged dog. Sweetest thing, a golden retriever mix. It would hop right up to you and rest its chin on your knee while you waited. \n\nSo, yeah, I don't know about the whole impulse thing. I just do what needs doing when it needs doing.\n\nDoctor: Would you describe yourself as someone who has always acted on impulse, even when you were younger?\n\nPatient: Well, younger... I mean, when you're young you do things, sure. But lately? Lately it's just been about getting things done. Like with the move. I just went ahead and put deposits down on all this garage work and bought equipment for the new place. Didn't even talk it over with my wife, which, well, she wasn't too happy about that. But you have to strike while the iron is hot! Just like at the plant. I've been rushing jobs there, trying to get everything finished up so I can focus on the move. People keep telling me I'm taking chances, moving too fast with the machinery, but they don't understand the schedule I'm on. \n\nI've been driving back and forth between the old house and the new one, too. Just back and forth, back and forth. The new house has this big oak tree in the front yard. Massive thing. Reminds me of the tree we had when I was a kid growing up on Elm Street. Ironically, it wasn't an elm tree, it was a maple. We used to tap it for syrup in the winter. My dad had these little metal buckets he'd hang on the spiles. You'd hear the drip, drip, drip all day if it was quiet enough. We'd boil it down on the stove and the whole house would smell sweet and sticky for a week. My mother hated it because it made the wallpaper peel in the kitchen. She had this yellow wallpaper with little roosters on it. So tacky, looking back on it, but that was the style then. Everything was roosters or apples. \n\nAnyway, what was I saying? Oh, right, the deposits. Yeah, I just paid 'em. You can't wait around for people to make up their minds, you know?\n\nDoctor: Would you say that acting on impulse has always been a part of your personality, even before this recent period of stress with the move?\n\nPatient: Well, no, not always. I mean, this whole thing, it's really just been the last month or so. Ever since we realized we were being forced out of the old house and had to start leaving. It's been a nightmare, honestly. The packing alone... you don't realize how much stuff you accumulate over thirty years until you have to put it all in cardboard boxes. \n\nAnd getting boxes, that's a whole ordeal now! You used to just go down to the grocery store and ask the manager for the egg crates. They were the best ones, thick cardboard, sturdy. The manager at the A&P, Mr. Henderson, he always saved them for me. He wore these thick glasses that made his eyes look huge, like an owl. He retired down to Florida, I think. Boca Raton or somewhere like that. A lot of people from around here end up in Florida. I could never do the humidity, though. Makes my joints ache just thinking about it. Plus, the bugs down there are the size of your fist! My brother-in-law lived in Tampa for a few years and he said he found a palmetto bug in his shoe once. Can you imagine? You go to put your shoe on and crunch! \n\nBut yeah, it's just been this last month with the house situation. Before that, I was just going to work, coming home, same as always.\n\nDoctor: Would you say that acting on impulse without thinking things through is something that you've always done, or is it something that has started happening more recently?\n\nPatient: Well, like I was trying to say, it's really just been this last month. Just scratched a groove right into the paper. I had to go back out to the truck to find one, and then I ended up finding that old flashlight I thought I lost back in November. The one with the heavy metal casing that takes the big D batteries. You don't see flashlights like that much anymore. Now everything is those tiny LED things. They're bright, sure, but they don't feel substantial in your hand, you know? If you had to break a window in an emergency, one of those little plastic things wouldn't do you any good. \n\nBut yeah, it's just been the last month or so, since the whole house thing started. Before that, everything was perfectly normal.\n\nDoctor: Would you say that acting on impulse is something that you've always done, even when you were younger, or is it something that has started happening more recently?\n\nPatient: I feel like we're going in circles here, Doc! You had to smack the dashboard right above the radio with the heel of your hand to get it to switch tracks. Jimmy actually broke his watch doing that once. \n\nSo, I don't know about changing over time or acting on impulse. I've always just kind of done what makes sense at the exact moment, you know? You just gotta keep moving.\n\nDoctor: Would you say that acting on impulse without thinking things through is something that you've done your whole life?\n\nPatient: Well, my whole life? I don't know if I'd say my *whole* life. I mean, what does it mean to think things through anyway? You can plan and plan and plan, and then it rains. \n\nLike when we were supposed to go to my sister's wedding back in '82. No, no, I just told you, it's not a part of my personality at all! I'm a planner. I've always been a planner. You don't make it to seventy-four by flying by the seat of your pants. You have to have a schedule, a routine.

And then I'm in the truck, driving back and forth between the old house and the new one, trying to beat the traffic on I-95. The guys at work said I was driving like a maniac, but they just don't understand how much I have to do! I've been making that drive for thirty years, I know every pothole on that highway. There's this one right near the exit for the diner—the one that makes the best blueberry pancakes, you know the place? My wife and I used to go there every Sunday after church. Anyway, I know what I'm doing. At work, they actually pulled me off the floor. It's a shame, really, because those machines need a certain touch. You can't just put anybody on a grinder. I remember when we got the new models back in '98, took me three weeks just to figure out the vibration patterns. You have to listen to the hum of the motor, you know? It sings to you if it's running right. \n\nBut anyway, yeah, work's a problem right now. And at home... well, my wife and the kids, they've basically cut me out of the loop. They don't trust me with the money anymore, after the garage deposits. And they don't want me driving, either. My wife hid my keys the other day! Can you believe that? Hid the keys to my own truck! You just gotta keep moving.\n\nDoctor: Would you say that acting on impulse without thinking things through is something that you've done your whole life?\n\nPatient: Well, my whole life? I don't know if I'd say my *whole* life. I mean, what does it mean to think things through anyway? You can plan and plan and plan, and then it rains. \n\nLike when we were supposed to go to my sister's wedding back in '82. We had the route all mapped out—this was before GPS, you know, when you had to use those big fold-out paper maps from the gas station. The ones you could never fold back up the right way. My wife used to get so mad when I'd just shove it in the glove compartment all crumpled up. The glove compartment on that old Buick LeSabre was huge, though. You could fit three flashlights, a tire gauge, and a whole box of tissues in there. We used to keep those little peppermints wrapped in the clear plastic in there too. They'd get all soft in the summer heat. \n\nAnyway, we had it all planned, and then the alternator went out right outside of Columbus. Just died on the highway. So much for thinking things through, right? Sometimes you just have to act on what's right in front of you. You just gotta fix the alternator or buy a new car. Actually, we ended up getting towed to this little shop where the mechanic had a three-legged dog. Sweetest thing, a golden retriever mix. It would hop right up to you and rest its chin on your knee while you waited. \n\nSo, yeah, I don't know about the whole impulse thing. I just do what needs doing when it needs doing.\n\nDoctor: Would you describe yourself as someone who has always acted on impulse, even when you were younger?\n\nPatient: Well, younger... I mean, when you're young you do things, sure. But lately? Lately it's just been about getting things done. Like with the move. I just went ahead and put deposits down on all this garage work and bought equipment for the new place. Didn't even talk it over with my wife, which, well, she wasn't too happy about that. But you have to strike while the iron is hot! Just like at the plant. I've been rushing jobs there, trying to get everything finished up so I can focus on the move. People keep telling me I'm taking chances, moving too fast with the machinery, but they don't understand the schedule I'm on. \n\nI've been driving back and forth between the old house and the new one, too. Just back and forth, back and forth. The new house has this big oak tree in the front yard. Massive thing. Reminds me of the tree we had when I was a kid growing up on Elm Street. Ironically, it wasn't an elm tree, it was a maple. We used to tap it for syrup in the winter. My dad had these little metal buckets he'd hang on the spiles. You'd hear the drip, drip, drip all day if it was quiet enough. We'd boil it down on the stove and the whole house would smell sweet and sticky for a week. My mother hated it because it made the wallpaper peel in the kitchen. She had this yellow wallpaper with little roosters on it. So tacky, looking back on it, but that was the style then. Everything was roosters or apples. \n\nAnyway, what was I saying? Oh, right, the deposits. Yeah, I just paid 'em. You can't wait around for people to make up their minds, you know?\n\nDoctor: Would you say that acting on impulse has always been a part of your personality, even before this recent period of stress with the move?\n\nPatient: Well, no, not always. I mean, this whole thing, it's really just been the last month or so. Ever since we realized we were being forced out of the old house and had to start leaving. It's been a nightmare, honestly. The packing alone... you don't realize how much stuff you accumulate over thirty years until you have to put it all in cardboard boxes. \n\nAnd getting boxes, that's a whole ordeal now! You used to just go down to the grocery store and ask the manager for the egg crates. They were the best ones, thick cardboard, sturdy. The manager at the A&P, Mr. Henderson, he always saved them for me. He wore these thick glasses that made his eyes look huge, like an owl. He retired down to Florida, I think. Boca Raton or somewhere like that. A lot of people from around here end up in Florida. I could never do the humidity, though. Makes my joints ache just thinking about it. Plus, the bugs down there are the size of your fist! My brother-in-law lived in Tampa for a few years and he said he found a palmetto bug in his shoe once. Can you imagine? You go to put your shoe on and crunch! \n\nBut yeah, it's just been this last month with the house situation. Before that, I was just going to work, coming home, same as always.\n\nDoctor: Would you say that acting on impulse without thinking things through is something that you've always done, or is it something that has started happening more recently?\n\nPatient: Well, like I was trying to say, it's really just been this last month. You know, since we got the news that we were being forced to start leaving the old house. It's not like I've been doing this my whole life! But when you have a deadline hanging over your head... \n\nSpeaking of deadlines, the post office has been an absolute nightmare with the change of address forms. You'd think in this day and age, with all the computers, they could just press a button and know where I live. But no, I had to fill out this little card, and the pen they had chained to the desk—why do they chain them? Who is stealing those cheap little plastic pens? Anyway, it was completely out of ink. Just scratched a groove right into the paper. I had to go back out to the truck to find one, and then I ended up finding that old flashlight I thought I lost back in November. The one with the heavy metal casing that takes the big D batteries. You don't see flashlights like that much anymore. Now everything is those tiny LED things. They're bright, sure, but they don't feel substantial in your hand, you know? If you had to break a window in an emergency, one of those little plastic things wouldn't do you any good. \n\nBut yeah, it's just been the last month or so, since the whole house thing started. Before that, everything was perfectly normal.\n\nDoctor: Would you say that acting on impulse is something that you've always done, even when you were younger, or is it something that has started happening more recently?\n\nPatient: I feel like we're going in circles here, Doc! Like I said, it's just been the last month. About a month, yeah. Ever since we found out we were being forced to start leaving the old house. It's not a lifelong habit, I promise you. \n\nThough, speaking of habits, I used to have this terrible habit of chewing on the end of my pencils when I was in college. Just gnawing them down to the metal part where the eraser used to be. I took a few classes over at the community college—business administration, thought I might want to run my own shop someday. Never panned out, ended up at the plant instead, grinding and polishing. But those pencils... my wife, well, my girlfriend at the time, she used to get so mad because I'd borrow her good drafting pencils and ruin them. She was studying architecture. She had this whole set of those Staedtler pencils, you know the blue ones? Beautiful things. They came in a little tin case that clicked when you shut it. I love a good tin case. You can use them for all sorts of things after the pencils are gone. Screws, nails, fishing lures. My grandfather had a whole wall of old tobacco tins in his garage filled with every size screw you could imagine. Prince Albert in a can! Remember that old joke? \"Do you have Prince Albert in a can? Well you better let him out!\" \n\nAnyway... yeah. Just a month. Since the house thing. That's it.\n\nDoctor: Can you think of any times before this last month when you acted on impulse without thinking things through?\n\nPatient: No, no, I can't think of anything like that before. I mean, I've always been a pretty steady guy. You work at the plant for forty years, you have to be steady. You can't just go doing things without thinking when you're working with those big industrial grinders. \n\nThose machines, let me tell you, they don't forgive mistakes. We had this one guy, Tommy... or was it Terry? Tommy, I think. Anyway, he got his sleeve caught in the polisher once because he wasn't paying attention. Ripped the whole shirt right off his back! He was lucky it was just the shirt. After that, they made us all wear these short-sleeved coveralls. Looked like a bunch of oversized mechanics walking around. They were this awful shade of green, too. Like pea soup. My wife hated washing them because the grease would never fully come out, and it would leave this ring around the inside of the washing machine. We had one of those old Maytags with the agitator in the middle that sounded like a jet engine taking off when it got to the spin cycle. Shook the whole laundry room. The dog used to hide under the kitchen table whenever she ran it. He was a good dog, part beagle, part something else. Howled at the mailman every single day for twelve years. \n\nBut no, I've never been one to just act on impulse. Not before all this house business, anyway.\n\nDoctor: Can you recall any instances from your childhood or younger years where you acted on impulse without thinking things through?\n\nPatient: Childhood? No, I really don't think so. I was a pretty cautious kid, all things considered. I didn't go jumping off roofs or doing crazy stunts or anything like that. \n\nI did have this old Schwinn bicycle, though. One of those with the big banana seats and the high handlebars—a Stingray, I think they called it. Mine was candy apple red. My dad bought it off a neighbor down the street, Mr. Henderson. Now, Mr. Henderson, he had the most incredible tomato garden you've ever seen in your life. He grew these massive beefsteak tomatoes, practically the size of a softball! He swore up and down that his secret was crushing up eggshells and mixing them with old coffee grounds into the dirt. \n\nI actually tried that myself years later when Mary and I got our first place, but it didn't do a lick of good for my tomatoes. All it did was attract raccoons. And let me tell you, raccoons are smart little devils. They have those little hands, like tiny burglars. One of them figured out how to unlatch the cooler we kept out on the back porch. Drank three whole cans of my A&W root beer and just left the empty cans sitting right there on the welcome mat! Can you believe that? The audacity of that animal. \n\nAnyway... what was the question? Oh, right, being young. Yeah, no, I was just a regular, careful kid. Never really did things without thinking about them first.\n\nDoctor: Can you recall any instances from before the last month where you acted on impulse and later regretted it?\n\nPatient: Doc, we keep going over this! No, nothing before this last month. I haven't done anything impulsive that I regretted, not before all this mess with the house. I've always been a think-before-you-leap kind of guy. \n\nYou know, speaking of leaping, my brother-in-law, Gary... he was the impulsive one. Oh boy, was he. One time, back in the eighties, he just up and bought a boat. Didn't tell my sister, didn't check the finances, just came home dragging this twenty-foot fiberglass thing behind his station wagon. It was a terrible idea. They lived in an apartment complex! They didn't even have a driveway to park it in. The landlord threw an absolute fit. \n\nGary ended up having to pay to keep it at this marina down by the lake, and I swear, it cost him more to dock the darn thing than he paid for the boat itself. We took it out maybe twice. The second time, the outboard motor just died right in the middle of the lake. We had to sit there for three hours waiting for the water patrol to tow us back in. Gary was so sunburnt by the time we got back, he looked like a boiled lobster. He had to slather himself in aloe vera for a week. My sister made him sell it the next month. Took a huge loss on it, too. \n\nBut me? No, I'm not like Gary. I don't buy boats without telling my wife. I'm careful. It's just been this last month with the house, that's all.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your tendency to act on impulse is something that has always been a part of your personality?\n\nPatient: No, no, I just told you, it's not a part of my personality at all! I'm a planner. I've always been a planner. You don't make it to seventy-four by flying by the seat of your pants. You have to have a schedule, a routine. \n\nLike my morning routine, right? I wake up at six-thirty every single day, rain or shine. I go down to the kitchen, I put on the coffee—Folgers, always Folgers, none of that fancy French roast nonsense they sell at the supermarket now. It tastes burnt, if you ask me. Well, like I keep saying, it's the move. It's only been going on for about a month, right since we were forced to start leaving the old house. You go to put your shoe on and crunch! \n\nBut yeah, it's just been this last month with the house situation. Before that, I was just going to work, coming home, same as always.\n\nDoctor: Would you say that acting on impulse without thinking things through is something that you've always done, or is it something that has started happening more recently?\n\nPatient: Well, like I was trying to say, it's really just been this last month. You know, since we got the news that we were being forced to start leaving the old house. It's not like I've been doing this my whole life! But when you have a deadline hanging over your head... \n\nSpeaking of deadlines, the post office has been an absolute nightmare with the change of address forms. You'd think in this day and age, with all the computers, they could just press a button and know where I live. But no, I had to fill out this little card, and the pen they had chained to the desk—why do they chain them? Who is stealing those cheap little plastic pens? Anyway, it was completely out of ink. Just scratched a groove right into the paper. I had to go back out to the truck to find one, and then I ended up finding that old flashlight I thought I lost back in November. The one with the heavy metal casing that takes the big D batteries. You don't see flashlights like that much anymore. Now everything is those tiny LED things. They're bright, sure, but they don't feel substantial in your hand, you know? If you had to break a window in an emergency, one of those little plastic things wouldn't do you any good. \n\nBut yeah, it's just been the last month or so, since the whole house thing started. Before that, everything was perfectly normal.\n\nDoctor: Would you say that acting on impulse is something that you've always done, even when you were younger, or is it something that has started happening more recently?\n\nPatient: I feel like we're going in circles here, Doc! Like I said, it's just been the last month. About a month, yeah. Ever since we found out we were being forced to start leaving the old house. It's not a lifelong habit, I promise you. \n\nThough, speaking of habits, I used to have this terrible habit of chewing on the end of my pencils when I was in college. Just gnawing them down to the metal part where the eraser used to be. I took a few classes over at the community college—business administration, thought I might want to run my own shop someday. Never panned out, ended up at the plant instead, grinding and polishing. But those pencils... my wife, well, my girlfriend at the time, she used to get so mad because I'd borrow her good drafting pencils and ruin them. She was studying architecture. She had this whole set of those Staedtler pencils, you know the blue ones? Beautiful things. They came in a little tin case that clicked when you shut it. I love a good tin case. You can use them for all sorts of things after the pencils are gone. Screws, nails, fishing lures. My grandfather had a whole wall of old tobacco tins in his garage filled with every size screw you could imagine. Prince Albert in a can! Remember that old joke? \"Do you have Prince Albert in a can? Well you better let him out!\" \n\nAnyway... yeah. Just a month. Since the house thing. That's it.\n\nDoctor: Can you think of any times before this last month when you acted on impulse without thinking things through?\n\nPatient: No, no, I can't think of anything like that before. I mean, I've always been a pretty steady guy. You work at the plant for forty years, you have to be steady. You can't just go doing things without thinking when you're working with those big industrial grinders. \n\nThose machines, let me tell you, they don't forgive mistakes. We had this one guy, Tommy... or was it Terry? Tommy, I think. Anyway, he got his sleeve caught in the polisher once because he wasn't paying attention. Ripped the whole shirt right off his back! He was lucky it was just the shirt. After that, they made us all wear these short-sleeved coveralls. Looked like a bunch of oversized mechanics walking around. They were this awful shade of green, too. Like pea soup. My wife hated washing them because the grease would never fully come out, and it would leave this ring around the inside of the washing machine. We had one of those old Maytags with the agitator in the middle that sounded like a jet engine taking off when it got to the spin cycle. Shook the whole laundry room. The dog used to hide under the kitchen table whenever she ran it. He was a good dog, part beagle, part something else. Howled at the mailman every single day for twelve years. \n\nBut no, I've never been one to just act on impulse. Not before all this house business, anyway.\n\nDoctor: Can you recall any instances from your childhood or younger years where you acted on impulse without thinking things through?\n\nPatient: Childhood? No, I really don't think so. I was a pretty cautious kid, all things considered. I didn't go jumping off roofs or doing crazy stunts or anything like that. \n\nI did have this old Schwinn bicycle, though. One of those with the big banana seats and the high handlebars—a Stingray, I think they called it. Mine was candy apple red. My dad bought it off a neighbor down the street, Mr. Henderson. Now, Mr. Henderson, he had the most incredible tomato garden you've ever seen in your life. He grew these massive beefsteak tomatoes, practically the size of a softball! He swore up and down that his secret was crushing up eggshells and mixing them with old coffee grounds into the dirt. \n\nI actually tried that myself years later when Mary and I got our first place, but it didn't do a lick of good for my tomatoes. All it did was attract raccoons. And let me tell you, raccoons are smart little devils. They have those little hands, like tiny burglars. One of them figured out how to unlatch the cooler we kept out on the back porch. Drank three whole cans of my A&W root beer and just left the empty cans sitting right there on the welcome mat! Can you believe that? The audacity of that animal. \n\nAnyway... what was the question? Oh, right, being young. Yeah, no, I was just a regular, careful kid. Never really did things without thinking about them first.\n\nDoctor: Can you recall any instances from before the last month where you acted on impulse and later regretted it?\n\nPatient: Doc, we keep going over this! No, nothing before this last month. I haven't done anything impulsive that I regretted, not before all this mess with the house. I've always been a think-before-you-leap kind of guy. \n\nYou know, speaking of leaping, my brother-in-law, Gary... he was the impulsive one. Oh boy, was he. One time, back in the eighties, he just up and bought a boat. Didn't tell my sister, didn't check the finances, just came home dragging this twenty-foot fiberglass thing behind his station wagon. It was a terrible idea. They lived in an apartment complex! They didn't even have a driveway to park it in. The landlord threw an absolute fit. \n\nGary ended up having to pay to keep it at this marina down by the lake, and I swear, it cost him more to dock the darn thing than he paid for the boat itself. We took it out maybe twice. The second time, the outboard motor just died right in the middle of the lake. We had to sit there for three hours waiting for the water patrol to tow us back in. Gary was so sunburnt by the time we got back, he looked like a boiled lobster. He had to slather himself in aloe vera for a week. My sister made him sell it the next month. Took a huge loss on it, too. \n\nBut me? No, I'm not like Gary. I don't buy boats without telling my wife. I'm careful. It's just been this last month with the house, that's all.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your tendency to act on impulse is something that has always been a part of your personality?\n\nPatient: No, no, I just told you, it's not a part of my personality at all! I'm a planner. I've always been a planner. You don't make it to seventy-four by flying by the seat of your pants. You have to have a schedule, a routine. \n\nLike my morning routine, right? I wake up at six-thirty every single day, rain or shine. I go down to the kitchen, I put on the coffee—Folgers, always Folgers, none of that fancy French roast nonsense they sell at the supermarket now. It tastes burnt, if you ask me. Anyway, I make my coffee, and I sit at the little table by the window and I read the paper. Well, I used to read the physical paper. Now they just deliver it on this tablet thing my daughter got me for Christmas a few years back. An iPad, she called it. \n\nI tell you, it took me three months just to figure out how to turn the darn thing on without accidentally taking a picture of my own forehead. Every time I tried to read the sports section, I'd swipe the wrong way and end up looking at a recipe for kale salad or something. Who eats kale? It tastes like lawn clippings. My neighbor, Mrs. Gable, she grows kale in her backyard. She tried to give me a whole bag of it once, said it was a \"superfood.\" I told her, \"Mrs. Gable, the only superfood I need is a good pork chop.\" \n\nShe makes a mean pork chop, actually. Bakes it with apples and onions. She brought some over when Mary passed... \n\nBut, uh, what were we talking about? Oh, my personality. No, I'm not an impulsive man. I plan things out. Always have.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your recent impulsivity is a result of the stress from the move or is it something that has been a part of your behavior for a long time?\n\nPatient: Well, like I keep saying, it's the move. It's only been going on for about a month, right since we were forced to start leaving the old house. Having to pack up all your things... it just gets to you. My daughter brought over all these cardboard boxes, the ones from the hardware store. They charge you three dollars a box now! Can you believe that? Used to be you could just go down to the liquor store or the grocery market and ask the manager for their empty boxes for free. The egg crates were the best ones, real sturdy bottoms. \n\nI used to bring home these heavy-duty plastic drums from the plant, too. I ran the industrial mixers and grinders for thirty-five years, making polishing compounds and abrasives. We went through a lot of containers. Whenever one got a little crack in it, my supervisor, Chuck—well, Charles, but everyone called him Chuck—he’d let me take them home. Chuck was a good guy. He had this old basset hound that used to sleep under his desk in the site office. Dog smelled like old Fritos and snored louder than the grinding machines, I swear. \n\nAnyway, I'd take those drums home and use them to store rock salt for the winter. We got terrible ice on the driveway at the old house. The new place they're putting me in doesn't even have a proper driveway, just this little paved strip. It's an insult, really. So, yeah, the stress of it all. It's just been this last month since they made us start clearing out the house. I wasn't like this before that.\n\nDoctor: Is it possible that you have always had some tendency towards acting on impulse, but it has only become more noticeable recently due to the stress of the move?\n\nPatient: I don't know why you keep asking me the same thing, Doc. No, it hasn't always been there! I've been telling you, it's just this last month. It all started when we were forced to start leaving the old house. About a month ago, that's it. Before that, nothing. \n\nI mean, moving is just... it's a nightmare. Especially when you don't want to go. My daughter, she means well, but she just came in and started putting tags on all my furniture. Green tags for the new place, red tags for the estate sale. Estate sale! Makes me sound like I'm already dead. \n\nShe tried to put a red tag on my favorite recliner. The brown leather one. I bought that chair back in '98. It's perfectly broken in. You sit in it, and it just hugs you, you know? It's got this little lever on the side that you pull, and it pops the footrest up. Well, the lever sticks a little bit now, you kind of have to jiggle it, but it works fine. I used to fall asleep in that chair every Sunday watching the football games. The Bears, usually. Though they haven't been worth watching in years. Not since Ditka. \n\nNow, Ditka, there was a guy who knew how to run things. You didn't see him letting people push him around or tell him where to live. He had that mustache... always looked like he was about to yell at somebody. I liked that about him. \n\nBut anyway, my daughter wanted to sell my chair! I told her, I said, \"If that chair doesn't go to the new place, I don't go to the new place.\" So she changed the tag to green. But it just goes to show you... the stress of it all. People trying to take your things. So, yeah, it's just been this last month. Since the move. That's all it is.\n\n[Instruction]\n- Ask about exactly ONE thing. Always have.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your recent impulsivity is a result of the stress from the move or is it something that has been a part of your behavior for a long time?\n\nPatient: Well, like I keep saying, it's the move. It's only been going on for about a month, right since we were forced to start leaving the old house. Having to pack up all your things... it just gets to you. My daughter brought over all these cardboard boxes, the ones from the hardware store. They charge you three dollars a box now! Can you believe that? Used to be you could just go down to the liquor store or the grocery market and ask the manager for their empty boxes for free. The egg crates were the best ones, real sturdy bottoms. \n\nI used to bring home these heavy-duty plastic drums from the plant, too. I ran the industrial mixers and grinders for thirty-five years, making polishing compounds and abrasives. We went through a lot of containers. Whenever one got a little crack in it, my supervisor, Chuck—well, Charles, but everyone called him Chuck—he’d let me take them home. Chuck was a good guy. He had this old basset hound that used to sleep under his desk in the site office. Dog smelled like old Fritos and snored louder than the grinding machines, I swear. \n\nAnyway, I'd take those drums home and use them to store rock salt for the winter. We got terrible ice on the driveway at the old house. The new place they're putting me in doesn't even have a proper driveway, just this little paved strip. It's an insult, really. So, yeah, the stress of it all. It's just been this last month since they made us start clearing out the house. I wasn't like this before that.\n\nDoctor: Is it possible that you have always had some tendency towards acting on impulse, but it has only become more noticeable recently due to the stress of the move?\n\nPatient: I don't know why you keep asking me the same thing, Doc. No, it hasn't always been there! I've been telling you, it's just this last month. It all started when we were forced to start leaving the old house. About a month ago, that's it. Before that, nothing. \n\nI mean, moving is just... it's a nightmare. Especially when you don't want to go. My daughter, she means well, but she just came in and started putting tags on all my furniture. Green tags for the new place, red tags for the estate sale. Estate sale! Makes me sound like I'm already dead. \n\nShe tried to put a red tag on my favorite recliner. The brown leather one. I bought that chair back in '98. It's perfectly broken in. You sit in it, and it just hugs you, you know? It's got this little lever on the side that you pull, and it pops the footrest up. Well, the lever sticks a little bit now, you kind of have to jiggle it, but it works fine. I used to fall asleep in that chair every Sunday watching the football games. The Bears, usually. Though they haven't been worth watching in years. Not since Ditka. \n\nNow, Ditka, there was a guy who knew how to run things. You didn't see him letting people push him around or tell him where to live. He had that mustache... always looked like he was about to yell at somebody. I liked that about him. \n\nBut anyway, my daughter wanted to sell my chair! I told her, I said, \"If that chair doesn't go to the new place, I don't go to the new place.\" So she changed the tag to green. But it just goes to show you... the stress of it all. People trying to take your things. So, yeah, it's just been this last month. Since the move. That's all it is.\n\nDoctor: Do you think you've always had a tendency to act on impulse, even before this recent period of stress with the move?\n\nPatient: Doc, are you even listening to me? I feel like a broken record here! No, I haven't always been like this. I've told you three times now, it's just been going on for about a month. Ever since they forced us to start leaving the old house. One month. That's it. \n\nI don't know why you doctors always have to dig and dig, trying to find something that isn't there. It reminds me of this dentist I had back in the eighties. Dr. Schuler. He was always poking around my gums with that sharp little metal hook, telling me I wasn't flossing enough. \"You have to floss, Richard, or your teeth are going to fall out.\" Well, I'm seventy-four and I still have most of my own teeth, so take that, Dr. Schuler. \n\nHe had this terrible waiting room, too. Smelled like old magazines and antiseptic. And he always played that elevator music. Muzak, they called it. Just this soft, featureless humming that made you want to fall asleep right there in the chair. Not like real music. Real music has a beat, it has soul. I used to go down to this little blues club on the South Side when I was younger. Buddy Guy played there once before he got really big. Now that was music. You could feel the bass right in your chest. \n\nI tried to play the guitar once, you know. Bought a cheap acoustic from a pawn shop. My fingers were always too calloused from the plant to press the strings down right, though. Working those industrial grinders, your hands get rough as sandpaper. You ever feel sandpaper, Doc? The heavy grit kind? That's what my palms felt like. \n\nBut no, to answer your question again, it's just been a month. Since they made me start packing up the house. That's all."
